items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

In many Indian cities, families are turning small balconies and rooftops into kitchen gardens. Using pots, old buckets and grow bags, they raise tomatoes, chillies, spinach and herbs. For some, the main attraction is fresh vegetables free of chemical sprays. Others enjoy the hour they spend each evening tending plants after a day at a screen. Children in such homes learn where food comes from and are often more willing to eat vegetables they have grown themselves. The costs are small, and many gardeners make their own compost from kitchen scraps, which also cuts the waste their homes send to landfills. A few housing societies have even set aside common terraces for residents who have no balcony of their own.
options: Kitchen gardens help children learn to eat more vegetables.
Kitchen gardens in cities now supply most of the vegetables that urban families eat.
The government should give free seeds to every city family that wants a kitchen garden.
City families are growing vegetables on balconies and rooftops at little cost, gaining fresh food, relaxation, lessons for their children and less household waste.
Housing societies are setting aside common terraces for all their residents.

steps: The paragraph describes a trend (home kitchen gardens) and its several benefits at low cost; only the correct option covers the trend and the range of benefits.
The children option is one detail; "most of the vegetables" overstates; free seeds is never mentioned.
solution.trap: The terrace option exaggerates "a few housing societies" into a general practice.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

A few years ago, a vegetable seller in a small town would have accepted only cash. Today, many such sellers display a QR code on their carts. Customers no longer need to carry change, and sellers do not have to worry about fake notes or about keeping cash safe at the end of the day. Each payment is recorded, which some vendors use to show banks a history of steady income when they apply for small loans. There are still problems: weak mobile networks can delay payments, and some older customers are not comfortable with phones. On the whole, however, digital payments have made daily trade simpler for both buyers and sellers.
options: Digital payments have completely replaced cash in India's small towns.
Vendors use their payment records to get small loans from banks.
Despite problems such as weak networks and some older customers' discomfort, QR-code payments have made small-scale trade easier for both sellers and buyers.
Weak mobile networks make digital payments useless for small traders.
The government should give free smartphones to older customers.

steps: The paragraph's conclusion is that digital payments have, on the whole, simplified trade despite some problems; the correct option keeps both the benefit and the qualification.
"Completely replaced cash" and "useless" distort the balance, and the loans option is a single detail.
solution.trap: The smartphone suggestion responds to a problem mentioned but is the reader's idea, not the author's.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Doctors often advise older people to walk for half an hour every day. Walking strengthens the heart, keeps joints flexible and helps control blood sugar and weight. It also improves balance, which reduces the risk of falls, a common cause of serious injury in old age. Unlike many forms of exercise, walking needs no equipment or fees and can be done in a park, a corridor or even around the house. Many older people also find that a regular morning walk with friends lifts their mood and gives shape to their day. Doctors do, however, suggest starting slowly and consulting them first if a person has heart or joint problems.
options: Walking in the morning is the best way for older people to make new friends.
Older people should avoid all other forms of exercise and only walk.
Walking reduces the risk of falls among older people.
Older people should join a gym, as walking alone is not enough to stay healthy.
A daily walk is a simple, free way for older people to improve their physical health and mood, though those with health problems should start slowly and take medical advice.

steps: The paragraph recommends walking for its many physical and mental benefits and its ease, with a caution for those with health problems; the correct option captures all three parts.
The falls option is one benefit only, and the gym option contradicts the paragraph.
solution.trap: "Avoid all other exercise" turns praise for walking into a prohibition the paragraph never makes.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

When a hill town in Himachal Pradesh banned single-use plastic bags, many shopkeepers expected their customers to complain. At first, some did. But the town council also handed out cloth bags at low cost and set up stalls where old bags could be returned. Within a year, the streets and drains were visibly cleaner, and fewer bags were found choking the town's streams. Shopkeepers reported that most customers now brought their own bags without being reminded. Tourists, too, praised the cleaner surroundings, and officials from nearby towns have visited to study the scheme. The council believes the ban worked because it came with easy alternatives, not just fines.
options: A hill town's ban on plastic bags succeeded, cleaning up the town and changing shoppers' habits, largely because it came with cheap and easy alternatives.
Tourists praised the hill town for its cleaner surroundings.
Customers in the hill town strongly opposed the plastic ban, and it failed.
Heavy fines are the most effective way to stop people using plastic bags.
Every town in India should ban plastic bags immediately.

steps: The paragraph reports that the ban worked and explains why (alternatives, not just fines); the correct option includes both the result and the reason.
The "failed" option contradicts the outcome; the fines option reverses the council's explanation.
solution.trap: "Every town should ban" is a recommendation the paragraph never makes.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

A government school in a dry district of Rajasthan used to depend on water tankers for several months each year. Three years ago, teachers and parents built a system to collect rainwater from the school's roof and store it in an underground tank. The tank now fills during the monsoon and provides enough water for drinking and cleaning for most of the year. The money once spent on tankers is used to buy books and sports equipment. Students have also learnt how the system works, and several have helped their families build similar tanks at home. Officials now plan to use the school as a model for others in the district.
options: The school now uses the money it saves on tankers to buy books and sports equipment.
Rainwater harvesting can end water shortages in every part of Rajasthan.
The government built an underground tank to supply water to the school.
The school closes during the summer because it has no water.
By harvesting rainwater from its roof, a school in a dry district ended its dependence on tankers, saved money and inspired students' families to do the same.

steps: The paragraph is about a school's rainwater system and its results; only the correct option names the system and its main effects.
The books option is one effect; "every part of Rajasthan" overgeneralises.
solution.trap: The government option gets the key fact wrong: teachers and parents built the system.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Heritage walks have become popular in cities such as Ahmedabad, Kolkata and Hyderabad. Led by local guides, small groups explore old neighbourhoods on foot, stopping at historic buildings, markets and street-food stalls. Participants say they learn stories about their city that they never found in textbooks. The walks also bring income to guides and to small shops along the route. Some residents, however, complain that large groups block narrow lanes and disturb daily life. Organisers have responded by limiting group sizes and choosing quieter hours. Several city governments now support such walks as a way of drawing attention to old buildings that need repair.
options: Heritage walks are mainly a way for visitors to sample street food.
Residents of old neighbourhoods have succeeded in stopping heritage walks.
Heritage walks earn city governments large sums for repairing old buildings.
Heritage walks bring income to guides and small shops.
Heritage walks, now popular in several cities, teach people local history and support small businesses, and organisers are addressing residents' complaints about crowding.

steps: The paragraph covers the walks' popularity, their benefits and the response to residents' complaints; the correct option covers all three.
The income option is one benefit only; the "stopping" option contradicts the paragraph.
solution.trap: City governments support the walks to draw attention to old buildings; nothing says the walks earn them money.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Many students preparing for examinations cut down on sleep to study longer. Research suggests this often backfires. During sleep, the brain sorts and stores what was learnt during the day, so a tired student may remember less of what he studied late into the night. Lack of sleep also slows reaction time, weakens concentration and makes people more irritable. Students who sleep seven to eight hours tend to perform better than those who study for extra hours but sleep for only four or five. Teachers therefore advise students to plan their studies so that they do not have to give up sleep before an examination.
options: Students should study for as many hours as possible before examinations.
Giving up sleep to study longer usually harms students' memory and concentration, so they should plan their studies to get enough sleep before examinations.
Lack of sleep makes people irritable.
Sleeping for more than eight hours guarantees top marks in examinations.
Schools should begin later in the morning so that students can sleep longer.

steps: The paragraph argues that losing sleep defeats the purpose of extra study, and it ends with advice to plan for sleep; the correct option has both.
The irritability option is a single detail, and "guarantees top marks" overstates the research.
solution.trap: Later school hours might help, but the paragraph never mentions them.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once everyday food in much of India. Over the decades, rice and wheat, backed by assured government purchase, pushed them out of fields and kitchens. Now millets are returning. They need far less water than rice, grow well on poor soils and withstand heat, which makes them suited to a warming climate. They are also rich in fibre and minerals. Food companies have begun selling millet biscuits, noodles and flour, and some states include millets in school meals. Farmers, however, say they will grow more only if they are sure of a fair price.
options: Millets are rich in fibre and minerals.
Millets have now replaced rice and wheat as India's main food grains.
The government should stop buying rice and wheat from farmers.
Millets, once pushed aside by rice and wheat, are making a comeback because they are hardy and nutritious, but farmers want an assured fair price before growing more.
Food companies have begun selling millet biscuits and noodles.

steps: The paragraph traces the decline and revival of millets, the reasons for the revival and the farmers' condition; the correct option covers all of it.
"Replaced rice and wheat" overstates a comeback, and the fibre and biscuit options are single details.
solution.trap: Stopping purchases of rice and wheat is not suggested anywhere.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Fraudsters are finding new ways to trick bank customers. Some call pretending to be bank officials and ask for an OTP to "update" an account. Others send messages with links to fake websites that look exactly like a bank's. A few even offer prizes or refunds that can be claimed only by sharing card details. Banks repeat that they never ask for OTPs, PINs or passwords by phone or message. Customers who receive such requests should refuse, report the number and, if money has been taken, inform the bank at once so that the account can be blocked. Quick reporting greatly improves the chances of recovering lost money.
options: Fraudsters use calls, fake links and false offers to steal bank details; customers should never share OTPs or passwords and should report any fraud to their bank at once.
Banks often ask customers for their OTPs to update their accounts.
Fraudsters send messages with links to fake websites.
Customers who lose money to fraud can never get it back.
Banks should stop using OTPs because they are unsafe.

steps: The paragraph describes fraud methods and then gives the key advice (never share, report quickly); the correct option combines them.
The first option contradicts the banks' statement, and "never get it back" contradicts the last sentence.
solution.trap: The fake-websites option is accurate but is only one of the tricks described.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

In remote villages where newspapers arrive late and television signals are weak, community radio stations have become an important source of information. Run by local volunteers, these stations broadcast in the local language or dialect. They share weather warnings, crop prices, health advice and news about government schemes. Farmers call in with questions that are answered by agricultural experts on air. Women's groups use the stations to discuss issues such as nutrition and children's education. Because the presenters are neighbours rather than strangers, listeners tend to trust what they hear. Many stations, however, struggle to raise the small sums they need to stay on air.
options: Farmers use community radio to ask experts about their crops.
Community radio has replaced newspapers and television in all Indian villages.
Locally run community radio has become a trusted and useful source of information for remote villages, although many stations find it hard to raise funds.
Community radio stations earn large profits from advertising.
The government should set up a television channel for every village.

steps: The paragraph shows why community radio matters to remote villages and notes its funding problem; the correct option includes both.
The farmers option is a detail, and "replaced … in all villages" overstates.
solution.trap: "Large profits" contradicts the struggle to raise even small sums.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

A city in Maharashtra replaced a quarter of its diesel buses with electric ones last year, as part of a plan to cut noise and pollution in the city centre. Commuters say the new buses are quieter and cleaner, and the air along the main routes has improved slightly. The city's transport body finds that electric buses cost more to buy but much less to run, because electricity is cheaper than diesel and the buses need less maintenance. The main problem has been charging: the depots needed new power connections, and some buses stood idle for weeks while chargers were installed. Officials still plan to make the entire fleet electric within five years.
options: Electric buses are cheaper than diesel buses both to buy and to run.
Some electric buses stood idle for weeks while chargers were installed.
The city has decided to go back to diesel buses because of charging problems.
A city's shift to electric buses has given it cleaner, quieter and cheaper-to-run transport despite early charging problems, and it plans to go fully electric within five years.
Every city in India should make its bus fleet electric at once.

steps: The paragraph weighs benefits and problems and ends with the plan to expand; the correct option gives the balance and the plan.
The idle-buses option is one detail, and the "back to diesel" option contradicts the plan.
solution.trap: The first option looks like a fair summary but gets the cost wrong: electric buses cost more to buy.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

For people in villages far from a hospital, seeing a specialist once meant a long and costly journey. Telemedicine is changing this. At a local health centre, a nurse connects the patient by video to a doctor in a city hospital, shares test reports and receives a prescription within minutes. Many centres now hold such sessions several times a week. Patients save on travel and lost wages, and doctors can advise many more people in a day. Telemedicine cannot replace every visit, since some conditions need a physical examination or surgery. But for routine follow-ups and common problems, it has made expert advice far easier to reach.
options: Telemedicine has made hospitals unnecessary in rural India.
Nurses at health centres can now carry out surgery with a doctor's help over video.
Telemedicine lets villagers consult city specialists from local health centres, saving time and money, though it cannot replace in-person care for every condition.
Patients who use telemedicine save on travel and lost wages.
Every village should have its own specialist hospital.

steps: The paragraph praises telemedicine for bringing specialists within reach but notes its limits; the correct option keeps both.
"Hospitals unnecessary" ignores the stated limits, and the savings option is a detail.
solution.trap: The surgery option twists the paragraph, which says surgery is exactly what telemedicine cannot provide.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Delivery riders, cab drivers and other app-based workers form a fast-growing part of India's workforce. The work is easy to enter: a smartphone, a vehicle and a few documents are often enough. Many value the freedom to choose their hours. Yet the same flexibility leaves them without the protections that regular employees enjoy. They are usually treated as "partners" rather than employees, so they have no fixed wages, paid leave or pension, and their earnings can change overnight when a platform alters its incentives. A few states have begun framing rules to give such workers accident insurance and a welfare fund financed partly by the platforms.
options: App-based workers enjoy fixed wages and pensions like regular employees.
Most app-based workers would prefer regular jobs with fixed hours.
App-based work is easy to join and flexible, but its workers lack the security of regular employment, and some states have begun framing rules to protect them.
Platforms can change the incentives they offer workers overnight.
State governments have barred platforms from treating workers as partners.

steps: The paragraph balances the appeal of app-based work against its insecurity and notes the first steps to protect workers; the correct option covers all three.
The first option contradicts the paragraph; the incentives option is one detail.
solution.trap: "Would prefer regular jobs" is an outside claim: the paragraph says many value the flexibility.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Air pollution is usually discussed as an environmental problem, but its heaviest cost may be economic. Polluted air causes asthma, heart disease and lung infections, which keep workers away from their jobs and children away from school. Families pay for medicines and hospital visits, often out of their own savings, and poorer households, who can least afford treatment, are usually the worst affected. Studies estimate that the losses in productivity and health care add up to a sizeable share of national output each year. Seen this way, spending on cleaner fuels, better public transport and stricter controls on industry is not a burden on growth but an investment that pays for itself.
options: Air pollution causes asthma, heart disease and lung infections.
Stricter controls on industry will slow down India's economic growth.
Because air pollution imposes heavy health and productivity costs, spending to reduce it should be seen as an economic investment rather than a burden.
Air pollution in India is caused mainly by vehicles in large cities.
Families should set aside savings to meet medical costs caused by pollution.

steps: The paragraph reframes pollution as an economic cost and concludes that fighting it is an investment; the correct option states exactly that.
The industry option reverses the conclusion, and the health option is only supporting detail.
solution.trap: The vehicles option adds a cause the paragraph never discusses.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Many educated women in India leave paid work after having children, and a large number never return. Surveys suggest that the main reason is not a lack of interest in working but the difficulty of finding safe, affordable childcare. In joint families, grandparents once looked after young children, but as more couples move to cities for jobs, that support is no longer available. Companies that have set up crèches at or near the workplace report that more mothers return after maternity leave. Experts argue that expanding reliable childcare, through both public centres and employers, could raise women's participation in the workforce significantly.
options: Most women leave their jobs because they lose interest in working after marriage.
Many women leave work after having children mainly because good childcare is hard to find, and expanding it could bring many more women back into the workforce.
In joint families, grandparents used to look after young children.
Companies should be fined if they do not employ enough women.
Crèches at the workplace have brought every mother back to work.

steps: The paragraph identifies lack of childcare as the main reason women leave work and proposes expanding it; the correct option captures cause and remedy.
The first option contradicts the survey finding, and the grandparents option is background.
solution.trap: "Every mother" inflates the report that "more mothers" return.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Clothes have never been cheaper, and people buy more of them than ever. Fast-fashion brands release new designs every few weeks, encouraging shoppers to treat clothes as disposable. Many garments are worn only a handful of times before being thrown away. The cost is hidden. Growing cotton needs large amounts of water, synthetic fabrics shed tiny plastic fibres when washed, and most discarded clothes end up in landfills. Some consumers are responding by buying fewer, better-made garments, repairing old ones or shopping at second-hand stores. Such choices, however, will have limited effect unless brands themselves take responsibility for what happens to their products after they are sold.
options: Cheap, fast-changing fashion carries hidden environmental costs, and although some consumers are buying more carefully, lasting change needs brands to take responsibility too.
Synthetic fabrics shed tiny plastic fibres when they are washed.
Careful consumer choices alone can solve the environmental problems of fast fashion.
Fast-fashion brands have started recycling all the clothes they sell.
Clothes are more expensive than ever, so people are buying fewer of them.

steps: The paragraph identifies the hidden costs of fast fashion and argues that consumer choices are not enough without brands; the correct option carries that argument.
"Consumer choices alone" contradicts the last sentence; the fibres option is a detail.
solution.trap: The recycling option invents an action by brands that the paragraph only calls for.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

India is still a young country, but it is ageing faster than many people realise. By the middle of this century, one in five Indians is expected to be over sixty, and many of them will need long-term medical care. Most older people today have no pension, because they worked on farms, in shops or in small businesses that offered none. Traditionally, children supported their parents, but smaller families and migration to cities have weakened that arrangement. Unless more workers begin saving for old age now, through pension schemes or other means, a large number of people could face their later years with neither income nor family support.
options: One in five Indians is already over the age of sixty.
Children should be required by law to support their parents.
Most older people in India receive a government pension.
Migration to cities has weakened the tradition of children supporting their parents.
As India ages and family support weakens, most older people lack pensions, so more workers must start saving for old age now to avoid widespread hardship later.

steps: The paragraph links rapid ageing, lack of pensions and weaker family support to a warning about saving now; the correct option captures that chain.
"Already over sixty" misreads a projection, and "receive a pension" contradicts the paragraph.
solution.trap: The migration option is true but is only one of the reasons behind the warning.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Paediatricians are increasingly concerned about the amount of time young children spend in front of screens. Toddlers who watch videos for hours may be slower to start talking, because language grows through conversation, not passive listening. Screens before bedtime can also disturb sleep. Doctors do not suggest banning screens altogether; a video call with grandparents or an educational programme watched together with a parent can be valuable. What matters, they say, is limiting time, choosing content carefully and ensuring that screens do not replace play, reading and talking with adults. For children under two, most advise avoiding screens except for video calls.
options: Doctors worry that too much screen time can harm young children's language and sleep, and they advise limiting and supervising it rather than banning it.
Doctors want screens banned for children of every age.
Screens before bedtime can disturb a child's sleep.
Educational programmes are always better for children than play.
Schools should teach children to use computers from the age of two.

steps: The paragraph states the doctors' concerns and their balanced advice (limit and supervise, do not ban); the correct option gives both.
The ban option contradicts "do not suggest banning screens altogether", and the sleep option is a detail.
solution.trap: The "better than play" option reverses the warning that screens must not replace play.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

When the Reserve Bank cuts its policy rate, borrowers expect loans to become cheaper at once. In practice, the effect reaches them slowly and unevenly. Banks raise much of their money through fixed deposits whose rates were set months earlier, so their costs do not fall immediately. Loans linked to an external benchmark adjust quickly, but older loans tied to a bank's internal rate may take much longer to change. This delay weakens the power of rate cuts to boost spending, since businesses and home buyers may postpone borrowing while they wait for cheaper loans. To speed things up, the central bank has pushed banks to link new loans to external benchmarks.
options: Rate cuts reach borrowers slowly because banks' costs adjust gradually and many loans follow internal rates, so the central bank is pushing for loans linked to external benchmarks.
Loans linked to external benchmarks change quickly when rates are cut.
Rate cuts make all loans cheaper as soon as they are announced.
Banks deliberately refuse to pass on rate cuts so as to raise their profits.
The central bank should stop cutting rates because the cuts have no effect.

steps: The paragraph explains why rate cuts pass through slowly and what the central bank is doing about it; the correct option has both the reasons and the response.
"As soon as announced" contradicts the paragraph, and "no effect" overstates a delay.
solution.trap: "Deliberately refuse … to raise profits" supplies a motive the paragraph never gives; it blames costs and loan structure.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Stretches of India's coastline, from Kerala to Odisha, are losing land to the sea. In some villages, homes and roads have already been washed away. Rising sea levels play a part, but much of the damage is local. Sand that rivers once carried to the coast is now trapped behind dams, and sand mining removes more from beaches. Sea walls built to protect one village often push the waves' energy along the shore, speeding up erosion at the next. Scientists argue that long-term solutions lie in restoring the natural flow of sediment, protecting mangroves and dunes, and planning construction away from vulnerable shores, rather than building ever more walls.
options: Rising sea levels are the only cause of coastal erosion in India.
Sea walls built to protect one village can speed up erosion at the next.
Coastal erosion in India is driven largely by local human activity, and experts favour natural, long-term remedies over building more sea walls.
All dams on Indian rivers should be removed to stop coastal erosion.
Sea walls are the most effective way to protect India's coasts.

steps: The paragraph argues that much erosion has local human causes and that natural remedies beat more walls; the correct option states both.
"Only cause" contradicts "much of the damage is local", and the sea-wall option is one detail.
solution.trap: Removing all dams goes far beyond "restoring the natural flow of sediment".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Children learn best when they are first taught in the language they speak at home. When a child enters school and hears only an unfamiliar language, much of the early years is spent struggling to follow instructions rather than learning to read and count. Studies from several states show that pupils taught in their mother tongue in the early grades read better and later pick up a second language more easily. Putting this into practice is not simple in a country with hundreds of languages, many without textbooks or trained teachers. Still, education experts argue that the effort pays off in stronger foundations for learning.
options: Teaching young children in their home language builds stronger foundations and even helps them learn other languages, though it is hard to put into practice across India's many languages.
Children should never be taught a second language in school.
Many Indian languages lack textbooks and trained teachers.
Children taught in their mother tongue find it harder to learn English later.
India should use a single language of instruction in all its schools.

steps: The paragraph argues for early mother-tongue teaching, admits the practical difficulty and concludes it is worth it; the correct option has all of this.
The "harder to learn" option contradicts the studies, and the textbooks option is only the difficulty.
solution.trap: "Never be taught a second language" misreads a point about the early grades as a lifelong rule.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

A large share of the fruit and vegetables grown in India spoils before it reaches consumers. The main reason is not a shortage of food but a shortage of cold storage and refrigerated transport close to farms. Produce is often carried in open trucks over long distances and stored in the heat, so tomatoes, mangoes and leafy vegetables rot within days. Farmers, forced to sell quickly, accept low prices at harvest, while consumers later pay high prices when supplies run short. Building small cold rooms near villages, many of them solar-powered, could reduce these losses and steady prices for both farmers and consumers.
options: India does not grow enough fruit and vegetables to feed its people.
Tomatoes, mangoes and leafy vegetables rot within days in the heat.
Much fresh produce spoils because cold storage and refrigerated transport near farms are lacking, and small village-level cold rooms could cut waste and steady prices.
Farmers deliberately hold back their produce to push up prices.
Large supermarket chains should be allowed to buy directly from all farmers.

steps: The paragraph names the cause of spoilage (missing cold chain near farms), its effect on prices and a remedy; the correct option includes all three.
The first option contradicts "not a shortage of food"; the tomatoes option is a detail.
solution.trap: The paragraph says farmers are forced to sell quickly, the opposite of holding produce back.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Small businesses often assume that hackers are interested only in banks and large companies. In fact, they are frequent targets precisely because their defences are weak. A single infected email attachment can lock a shop's billing system until a ransom is paid, and stolen customer data can destroy years of goodwill. Many owners discover an attack only when customers complain. Most attacks exploit simple lapses: weak passwords, outdated software and staff who click on suspicious links. Basic steps such as regular backups, automatic updates and short training sessions for employees cost little, yet they block most attacks. For a small firm, prevention is far cheaper than recovery.
options: Hackers are interested mainly in banks and large companies.
Small businesses are frequent targets of cyber-attacks because their defences are weak, but cheap, basic precautions can prevent most attacks.
Small businesses should hire full-time security experts to protect their systems.
Weak passwords are a common cause of cyber-attacks.
No precaution can protect a small business from a determined hacker.

steps: The paragraph corrects a false belief (small firms are safe) and says cheap basic steps block most attacks; the correct option carries both points.
The first option repeats the belief the paragraph rejects; the passwords option is one detail.
solution.trap: Full-time security experts contradict the paragraph's stress on cheap, basic steps.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

India's tiger population has grown steadily in recent years, a success credited largely to protected reserves and stricter action against poaching. The growth, however, has brought a new challenge. As tigers multiply and their reserves fill up, more of them stray into farmland and villages, killing cattle and occasionally people. Such conflict can quickly turn local communities against conservation, and in some areas villagers who lost cattle have struck back at the animals. Wildlife officials therefore stress quick compensation for losses, corridors that connect reserves, and involving villagers in protection work, so that people living near forests share in the benefits of conservation rather than only its costs.
options: Tiger numbers in India are falling because of increased poaching.
Tigers that stray into villages sometimes kill cattle.
The recovery of India's tigers has increased conflict with nearby villagers, so officials stress measures that make communities partners in conservation rather than its victims.
Tigers that stray into villages should be moved to zoos.
Protected reserves are now large enough to hold all of India's tigers.

steps: The paragraph's point is that success has created conflict, and that the answer is to give villagers a stake; the correct option covers both.
The falling-numbers option contradicts the paragraph, and the cattle option is a detail.
solution.trap: "Reserves large enough" contradicts "their reserves fill up".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

When schools shifted to online classes during the pandemic, the change exposed a sharp divide. Children in homes with fast internet and a laptop each continued to learn, while many others shared one phone among siblings or had no device at all. In some villages, students climbed hills or trees to catch a signal. Teachers, too, struggled to keep track of pupils they could not see. Surveys later found that the learning gap between richer and poorer children widened during this period. The experience showed that technology can extend education only when access to devices and connectivity is fairly shared; otherwise it deepens existing inequalities.
options: Online classes improved learning for all children during the pandemic.
The move to online schooling widened learning gaps because access to devices and the internet was unequal, showing that technology helps education only when access is fair.
Some village students climbed hills to catch a mobile signal.
Schools should permanently replace classroom teaching with online classes.
Online education should be given up because it always increases inequality.

steps: The paragraph uses the pandemic experience to make a conditional point: technology helps only with fair access. The correct option keeps that condition.
"Improved learning for all" contradicts the widened gap; the hills option is a detail.
solution.trap: "Always increases inequality" drops the condition "otherwise" and turns it into a blanket claim.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Geographical Indication (GI) tags identify products that owe their quality or reputation to a particular place, such as Darjeeling tea or Kanchipuram silk. The tag stops others from selling imitations under the same name, and it can help genuine producers command higher prices. In practice, the benefits have been uneven. Many artisans do not know their product has been tagged, few register as authorised users, and action against fakes, especially online, is weak. Buyers, for their part, often cannot tell a genuine product from a copy. Experts say GI tags will fulfil their promise only if they are backed by awareness among producers, strong marketing and action against counterfeits.
options: GI tags can protect place-linked products and raise producers' earnings, but their benefits have been limited by low awareness, few registrations and weak enforcement.
Darjeeling tea and Kanchipuram silk are protected by GI tags.
GI tags have put an end to the sale of imitation products in India.
GI tags are of no use to artisans and should be abolished.
The government should buy all GI-tagged products directly from artisans.

steps: The paragraph sets the promise of GI tags against their uneven results and says what is needed; the correct option covers the promise and the shortfall.
"Put an end to imitations" contradicts "action against fakes … is weak", and the Darjeeling option is only an example.
solution.trap: "No use … abolished" turns a call for better support into rejection.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Floods in Indian cities are often blamed on unusually heavy rain, but the rain is only part of the story. Lakes and wetlands that once soaked up excess water have been filled in and built over. Natural drainage channels have been blocked by roads and buildings, and storm-water drains are often clogged with plastic and silt. As a result, even ordinary monsoon showers can bring traffic to a halt. Planners argue that cities must protect their remaining water bodies, keep drains clean and leave more open, unpaved ground where water can seep in. Otherwise, each monsoon will bring the same damage.
options: Heavy rain is the only reason Indian cities flood.
Storm-water drains in cities are often clogged with plastic.
Cities should stop all new construction to prevent floods.
Indian cities rarely flood, even during heavy rain.
Urban flooding in India owes as much to lost lakes, blocked channels and clogged drains as to heavy rain, and planners call for protecting water bodies and drainage.

steps: The paragraph shifts the blame from rain to the loss of natural and built drainage, and proposes remedies; the correct option has cause and remedy.
"Only reason" contradicts the paragraph; the plastic option is one detail.
solution.trap: Stopping all construction is far more extreme than anything the planners propose.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Many Indian schools treat sport as a break from real learning, and physical education periods are often the first to be cut when examinations approach. In some schools, the playground itself has given way to new classrooms. Research suggests this is a mistake. Regular physical activity improves attention, memory and mood, and pupils who play sport often perform as well as or better than those who do not. Team games also teach cooperation, discipline and how to handle defeat, lessons that classrooms struggle to provide. Giving sport a protected place in the timetable, experts say, would benefit children's academic results as well as their health and character.
options: Pupils who play sport always score higher marks than those who do not.
Team games teach cooperation and discipline.
Schools should hire former athletes as sports teachers.
Schools wrongly treat sport as a distraction; it supports academic performance as well as health and character, and it deserves a protected place in the timetable.
Examinations matter more than sport, so sports periods should be cut before them.

steps: The paragraph argues against cutting sport, gives its academic and personal benefits and ends with a recommendation; the correct option includes all of it.
The last option states the practice the paragraph calls a mistake; the team-games option is a detail.
solution.trap: "Always score higher" overstates "as well as or better than".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Street vendors are a familiar part of Indian cities, selling everything from vegetables to snacks at prices that suit ordinary households. City authorities often treat them as a nuisance that blocks footpaths, and periodic eviction drives destroy their goods and livelihoods. Yet vendors meet a real demand, and many residents rely on them. For many people who migrate to cities, vending is also the easiest way to earn a living. A law passed some years ago requires cities to survey vendors, issue licences and set aside vending zones. Where it has been implemented, conflict has fallen and footpaths are clearer. In many cities, however, the surveys remain incomplete and evictions continue.
options: Street vendors are a nuisance and should be removed from footpaths.
Street vendors meet a real need, and a law meant to regulate rather than evict them has worked where applied, but its implementation remains patchy.
The law has ended evictions of street vendors in every Indian city.
Vendors sell vegetables and snacks at low prices.
Street vendors should be moved to large indoor markets outside the city.

steps: The paragraph defends vendors' role, credits the law where it is applied and notes weak implementation; the correct option has all three.
"Ended evictions in every city" contradicts the last sentence; the prices option is a detail.
solution.trap: The nuisance view is the authorities' attitude, which the paragraph argues against, not its conclusion.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Antibiotics are widely used in poultry farming, not only to treat sick birds but also to make healthy ones grow faster, and many such drugs are bought without a prescription. This routine use helps create bacteria that resist the drugs. Such bacteria can spread to people through undercooked meat, farm workers and waste that enters soil and water. When they cause infections in humans, the usual medicines may fail. Several countries have banned the use of antibiotics to promote growth in animals, and India has restricted some of the most important ones. Health experts say stricter monitoring on farms is needed if these medicines are to remain effective.
options: Antibiotics make healthy poultry birds grow faster.
People should stop eating chicken to avoid drug-resistant infections.
India has banned every use of antibiotics in poultry farming.
Routine antibiotic use in poultry breeds drug-resistant bacteria that can reach humans, so experts call for stricter control to keep the medicines effective.
Drug-resistant bacteria can easily be killed with the usual medicines.

steps: The paragraph traces the chain from farm use to human risk and ends with a call for stricter monitoring; the correct option follows that chain.
"Banned every use" overstates "restricted some", and the last option contradicts the paragraph.
solution.trap: Giving up chicken is the reader's solution, not the experts' recommendation.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

When an all-weather road reaches a village, the change goes far beyond easier travel. Farmers can take their produce to larger markets and get better prices instead of selling to the nearest trader, and village shops find it easier to restock. Children, especially girls, attend secondary school more regularly when it is a short bus ride away. Pregnant women reach hospitals in time, and doctors and teachers are more willing to work in the village. Studies of a national rural roads programme found that connected villages saw higher incomes and more non-farm jobs. Maintaining these roads after they are built, however, remains a weak point.
options: All-weather roads help farmers get better prices for their produce.
Rural roads have ended poverty in every village they connect.
Villages should build their own roads without government help.
All-weather roads bring villages wide economic, educational and health benefits, though keeping the roads in good repair remains a problem.
Rural roads have made little difference to village life.

steps: The paragraph lists the broad benefits of rural roads and ends with the maintenance problem; the correct option includes both.
The prices option is one benefit; "ended poverty" overstates "higher incomes".
solution.trap: "Little difference" contradicts the opening sentence.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

The shift to working from home during the pandemic was expected by many to be temporary. Several years later, a large number of companies have settled on a hybrid model, with employees in the office for part of the week. Workers value the time saved on commuting and the flexibility to manage family responsibilities. Employers, for their part, report that routine tasks are done just as well at home, but that training new staff and building team spirit are harder without face-to-face contact. The hybrid model is an attempt to capture the benefits of both arrangements. Some firms have even redesigned their offices around meeting rooms rather than rows of desks.
options: Most companies have returned to full-time work in the office.
Hybrid work has become common because it combines the flexibility and savings of working from home with the training and team-building advantages of the office.
Employees save time by not commuting to the office.
Working from home makes employees less productive at every kind of task.
The government should require all companies to adopt hybrid work.

steps: The paragraph explains why the hybrid model has settled in: it balances the advantages of home and office. The correct option states that balance.
"Returned to full-time office work" contradicts the paragraph; the commuting option is one advantage.
solution.trap: "Less productive at every task" contradicts "routine tasks are done just as well at home".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Savers who keep money in fixed deposits often judge their returns by the interest rate printed on the receipt. What matters, however, is the real return: the interest earned minus inflation. When a deposit pays 6 per cent while prices rise by 7 per cent, the saver is actually losing purchasing power, even though the balance in his account keeps growing. Tax on the interest widens the loss further. This is one reason many households have moved part of their savings into assets such as equity mutual funds, which carry more risk but have historically offered returns above inflation over long periods. Deposits still suit money that may be needed at short notice.
options: Fixed deposits always lose money and should be avoided by every saver.
Equity funds are safer than fixed deposits and always beat inflation.
Tax on interest reduces the return a saver earns on a deposit.
Banks should raise deposit rates above inflation to protect savers.
Savers should judge deposits by their return after inflation and tax, which can be negative; this helps explain why some savings have moved to riskier assets that have beaten inflation over time.

steps: The paragraph's core point is that the real, post-inflation return is what counts, and that this explains the shift into riskier assets; the correct option states both.
"Always lose money" ignores the conditional example and the closing note that deposits still have a use.
solution.trap: The equity option inverts "more risk" into "safer" and turns "historically … over long periods" into "always".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

People often stick with whatever option has been set for them by default. When employees are automatically enrolled in a pension plan and must opt out if they do not want it, far more of them end up saving than when they must actively sign up. The choice is the same in both cases; only the default differs. Governments and companies have begun using such "nudges" to encourage behaviour such as saving, organ donation and paying taxes on time. Critics worry that nudges can be used to manipulate people. Supporters reply that some default must always exist, so it might as well be one that serves people's interests.
options: Automatic enrolment leads far more employees to save for their pensions.
Nudges force people to save by taking away their freedom to choose.
Because people tend to accept defaults, setting helpful defaults can change behaviour a great deal; critics fear manipulation, but supporters argue that some default is unavoidable anyway.
Governments should make organ donation compulsory for every citizen.
Critics have proved that nudges are always used to manipulate people.

steps: The paragraph explains the power of defaults, their use as nudges and the debate over them; the correct option covers the principle and both sides.
The pension option is only the illustrating example.
solution.trap: "Force … taking away freedom" contradicts the example: employees can still opt out, since "the choice is the same".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Heatwaves kill quietly. Unlike floods or cyclones, they destroy no buildings, so deaths are often recorded as heart attacks or strokes rather than as the result of heat. After a severe heatwave caused hundreds of deaths in Ahmedabad in 2010, the city drew up a heat action plan. It issues early warnings, keeps parks and public buildings open as cooling centres, changes working hours for outdoor labourers and trains health workers to spot heatstroke. Deaths in later heatwaves fell sharply. Many other cities have since prepared similar plans, though experts note that several exist only on paper and are not backed by funds or staff.
options: Heatwaves destroy buildings and are therefore easy to measure.
Heatwaves are an under-recognised killer; Ahmedabad's heat action plan showed that simple preparations save lives, and many cities have copied it, though often without real resources.
Ahmedabad keeps its parks open as cooling centres during heatwaves.
Every Indian city now has a fully funded heat action plan.
Outdoor work should be banned in summer throughout India.

steps: The paragraph moves from the hidden danger of heat to a successful local plan and its uneven spread; the correct option keeps all three steps.
The parks option is one measure; "fully funded" contradicts "exist only on paper".
solution.trap: A summer ban on outdoor work goes far beyond "changes working hours for outdoor labourers".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

In several states, farmers receive electricity for irrigation free or at a nominal flat rate. The policy was meant to support farm incomes, and it did help spread irrigation. But because pumping more water costs the farmer nothing extra, there is little reason to use it carefully. Water tables in these states have fallen steeply, forcing farmers to dig deeper borewells and buy more powerful pumps, which raises their costs. Economists suggest that farmers could be paid a fixed cash subsidy while being charged for the power they actually use, so that saving water and electricity would put money in their pockets. Farmers' groups, however, fear that such payments may not keep pace with costs.
options: Free electricity for farmers has had only good effects.
Farmers have had to dig deeper borewells as water tables fall.
Farmers should pay the full cost of electricity with no subsidy at all.

Free farm power helped spread irrigation but encourages overuse of groundwater that ends up raising farmers' costs; economists propose a cash subsidy with charges for actual use, though farmers have doubts.
Farmers waste water on purpose to harm their neighbours.

steps: The paragraph shows how a well-meant subsidy backfired, proposes a redesign and notes farmers' worry; the correct option has all of it.
The borewells option is one consequence; "only good effects" ignores the falling water tables.
solution.trap: The proposal keeps a cash subsidy; "no subsidy at all" distorts it.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Most Indian workers are employed in the informal sector, in small workshops, farms and shops that are not registered and do not keep formal accounts. Such firms are flexible and create jobs quickly, but they rarely grow. Without records, they cannot borrow from banks; without loans, they cannot invest in the machines that raise productivity. Their workers, meanwhile, lack contracts and social security. Measures such as digital payments and simpler tax registration have begun to bring some of these firms into the formal economy. The challenge is to do so without burdening them with compliance costs so heavy that they are driven out of business.
options: Informal firms create jobs but stay small and unprotected because they lack records and credit; formalisation is under way but must avoid costs that would destroy them.
Informal firms are inefficient and should be shut down.
Digital payments have brought all small firms into the formal economy.
Workers in the informal sector lack contracts and social security.
Banks should lend to informal firms without asking for any records.

steps: The paragraph explains why informal firms stay small, notes progress towards formalisation and warns about its cost; the correct option covers all three.
"All small firms" overstates "some of these firms"; the workers option is one detail.
solution.trap: "Shut down" contradicts the paragraph's concern about driving these firms out of business.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

A single study, however striking its results, rarely settles a scientific question. Findings may arise by chance, from errors in measurement or from a sample that happens to be unusual. That is why scientists place great weight on replication: when other teams repeat an experiment independently and obtain similar results, confidence in the finding grows. In recent years, attempts to repeat well-known studies in psychology and medicine have often failed, prompting journals to encourage researchers to share their data and methods. The episode is less a crisis than a reminder that science corrects itself only when its results are checked.
options: A finding becomes reliable only when independent teams can repeat it; recent failures to do so are prompting greater openness and show that science depends on such checking.
Most published scientific studies are false and cannot be trusted.
Journals now encourage researchers to share their data and methods.
Psychology is not a real science because its results cannot be repeated.
A single striking study is usually enough to settle a scientific question.

steps: The paragraph argues for replication, cites recent failures and treats them as a healthy reminder; the correct option keeps that reading.
"Most studies are false" turns "less a crisis than a reminder" into a crisis.
solution.trap: The psychology option draws a sweeping conclusion the author never makes.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Indian farmers use far more urea, a nitrogen fertiliser, than their soils need, largely because its price is kept low by subsidies while other fertilisers cost more. The imbalance harms the soil. Over time, too much nitrogen and too little phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients reduce yields, so farmers apply still more urea to get the same harvest. Surplus nitrogen also seeps into groundwater and releases greenhouse gases. Soil testing can tell farmers exactly what their fields lack, but experts argue that such advice will be followed widely only if the price signals that push farmers towards urea are also corrected.
options: Urea is the only fertiliser that Indian soils need.
Surplus nitrogen seeps into groundwater and releases greenhouse gases.
Farmers should give up chemical fertilisers entirely and farm organically.
Cheap, subsidised urea has led to its overuse, harming soils, yields and the environment; soil testing helps, but lasting change needs the pricing that favours urea to be corrected.
Soil testing alone will solve the problem of fertiliser imbalance.

steps: The paragraph traces overuse of urea to its pricing, lists the harm and argues that advice must be matched by price reform; the correct option has cause, harm and remedy.
"Soil testing alone" contradicts the final sentence.
solution.trap: Organic farming is never proposed; the paragraph wants a better balance of fertilisers, not none.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Metro rail lines are expensive to build, and fares rarely cover their costs. Yet a new line usually raises the value of land and buildings near its stations, sometimes sharply. Owners gain from this rise without having paid anything towards the project that caused it. Some cities have begun to capture part of this gain to fund transport, through extra charges on new development near stations or by allowing taller buildings in exchange for fees. Supporters argue that this is fair as well as practical, since those who benefit most from the metro would help to pay for it. Critics worry that the charges may be passed on to home buyers.
options: Since metro lines raise nearby property values, some cities are tapping part of this gain to help fund transport, an approach its supporters see as fair and practical, though critics fear the cost will reach home buyers.
Metro fares should be raised until they cover the full cost of building the lines.
New metro lines usually lower the value of land near their stations.
Some cities allow taller buildings near metro stations in exchange for fees.
Property owners near stations pay the entire cost of building metro lines.

steps: The paragraph sets out the idea of capturing land-value gains to fund metros, with the argument for and against; the correct option covers both.
The taller-buildings option is one method only; "lower the value" contradicts the paragraph.
solution.trap: "Part of this gain" becomes "the entire cost" in the last option.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Rural India faces a persistent shortage of doctors, even as the number of medical graduates rises every year. Few young doctors want to work in villages, where facilities are poor, specialist support is distant and their own children would have limited schooling. Compulsory rural service has been tried in several states, but many graduates pay the penalty rather than serve. Some states have had better results by offering higher pay, preference in postgraduate admissions and decent housing, and by training local students, who are more likely to stay. Experts conclude that incentives and better working conditions work better than compulsion.
options: India produces too few medical graduates to staff its hospitals.
Compulsory rural service has solved the shortage of doctors in villages.
Doctors avoid rural posts mainly because of poor conditions, and experience suggests that incentives and better facilities attract them more effectively than compulsory service.
Some states give rural doctors preference in postgraduate admissions.
Private hospitals should be required to open branches in villages.

steps: The paragraph explains why doctors avoid villages and compares compulsion with incentives, favouring incentives; the correct option states that conclusion.
"Solved the shortage" contradicts the failure of compulsory service.
solution.trap: The first option misreads the problem: graduates are increasing; the shortage is in villages.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Hill towns such as Manali and Mussoorie receive far more visitors each summer than their roads, water supply and waste systems were built to handle. The result is traffic jams stretching for kilometres, water shortages for residents and heaps of garbage on the slopes. Tourism brings income that local people depend on, so few want to turn visitors away. Some planners propose limiting the number of vehicles entering a town each day, charging a green fee and spreading visitors across the year and across lesser-known places. The aim is not to reduce tourism but to keep it within limits that the hills can bear.
options: Planners want to ban tourists from hill towns during the summer.
Overcrowding strains hill towns' infrastructure and environment, and planners propose managing visitor numbers so that tourism stays within the hills' limits without being cut back.
Garbage is piling up on the slopes of popular hill towns.
Tourism brings little income to the people of the hills.
A new airport should be built near every hill town.

steps: The paragraph describes the strain from too many visitors and proposes managing, not reducing, tourism; the correct option keeps that distinction.
The ban option contradicts "the aim is not to reduce tourism"; the garbage option is a detail.
solution.trap: "Little income" contradicts "income that local people depend on".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Millions of Indians have no credit history because they have never taken a formal loan. Lenders, unable to judge them, either refuse them credit or charge high rates, so they cannot build the history they lack. Some lenders are now trying to break this circle by using other data, such as records of utility bill payments, mobile recharges and digital transactions, to judge whether a first-time borrower is likely to repay. This could bring many people into formal credit. It also raises concerns: such data may be collected without proper consent, and poorly designed models may unfairly exclude certain groups.
options: People with no credit history are usually unwilling to repay their loans.
Lenders use records of mobile recharges to judge first-time borrowers.
Alternative data will give everyone access to cheap credit without any risk.
The government should guarantee every loan to a first-time borrower.
Alternative data could help lenders assess people with no credit history and widen access to loans, but it raises concerns about consent and unfair exclusion.

steps: The paragraph presents a problem (no history, no credit), a possible solution (alternative data) and its risks; the correct option contains all three.
"Without any risk" ignores the concerns in the last sentence; the mobile option is one example.
solution.trap: The first option confuses "no history" with "unwilling to repay".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

India produces enough grain to feed its population, yet many people suffer from what nutritionists call hidden hunger: a lack of vitamins and minerals despite eating enough calories. A diet made up largely of rice or wheat can fill the stomach while leaving the body short of iron, zinc and vitamin A. The effects, such as anaemia, weaker immunity and stunted growth in children, are not always visible but are costly, both for families and for the economy. Fortifying staple foods with key nutrients, promoting a more varied diet and growing crop varieties bred to be richer in minerals are among the remedies being tried.
options: Many Indians get enough calories but too few micronutrients, with serious if unseen effects, and remedies being tried include fortification, a more varied diet and mineral-rich crops.
India does not produce enough grain to feed its people.
Anaemia is a common result of a lack of iron.
Eating more rice and wheat will solve the problem of hidden hunger.
Fortified foods are unsafe and should not be sold.

steps: The paragraph defines hidden hunger, explains its cause and effects, and lists remedies; the correct option compresses all of that.
The first option contradicts the opening, and the anaemia option is one effect.
solution.trap: "More rice and wheat" repeats the cause of the problem as its cure.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

When a smartphone or washing machine breaks down, owners increasingly find that repairing it is difficult or impossible. Manufacturers may refuse to sell spare parts, withhold repair manuals or design products so that a single faulty part means replacing the whole unit. This pushes consumers to buy new products sooner and adds to the growing heap of electronic waste. A movement known as the *right to repair* seeks rules requiring companies to make parts, tools and information available to owners and independent repair shops. Manufacturers argue that unauthorised repairs can compromise safety, but supporters counter that this concern can be addressed without blocking repair altogether.
options: Unauthorised repairs are unsafe, so only manufacturers should repair their products.
The amount of electronic waste is growing rapidly.
The right-to-repair movement wants manufacturers to stop making new products.
Manufacturers often make repair hard, pushing people to replace goods and adding to e-waste; the right-to-repair movement seeks rules to make repair possible, despite companies' safety objections.
Consumers should buy only products that carry a lifetime guarantee.

steps: The paragraph describes barriers to repair, their effects and the movement to remove them, with the manufacturers' objection; the correct option has all of these.
The first option adopts the manufacturers' side as the conclusion, which the paragraph rebuts.
solution.trap: The e-waste option is one effect; the "stop making new products" option invents an aim.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Much of India's agricultural research and public spending has focused on irrigated land, where the green revolution raised yields of rice and wheat dramatically. Yet more than half the country's cropped area depends on rain, and it is here that most poor farmers live. Yields on rain-fed land remain low and uncertain, and farmers there are the most exposed to erratic weather. Researchers argue that improved seeds for pulses and millets, better ways of conserving soil moisture and crop insurance suited to local conditions could lift these farms. The gains, they say, would be large precisely because this land has so far received so little attention.
options: The green revolution raised yields of rice and wheat on irrigated land.
Irrigated land should receive no further public spending.
Rain-fed land now gives higher yields than irrigated land.
Erratic weather makes it impossible to raise yields on rain-fed land.
Rain-fed farming, where most poor farmers work, has been neglected compared with irrigated land, and targeted research and support could bring large gains there.

steps: The paragraph contrasts attention to irrigated land with neglect of rain-fed land and argues that the latter offers big gains; the correct option states that.
The green-revolution option is background; "impossible to raise yields" contradicts the researchers.
solution.trap: Arguing for more attention to rain-fed land is not the same as cutting all spending on irrigated land.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Competitive entrance examinations were designed to select students fairly on merit. Over time, however, a large coaching industry has grown up around them, training students to recognise question patterns and solve problems at speed. Families spend heavily, and teenagers often move to coaching hubs far from home, where they study under intense pressure. Critics argue that the system now rewards the ability to pay for coaching and to practise endlessly as much as genuine understanding. Some suggest reducing the stakes of a single examination, for instance by giving weight to school performance, so that students have less reason to spend their teenage years in coaching classes.
options: Entrance examinations should be abolished and admissions decided by lottery.
The coaching industry built around entrance examinations has made them costly and stressful and may reward practice and money over understanding, prompting calls to lower the stakes of a single test.
Many teenagers move to coaching hubs far from home.
Coaching has made entrance examinations fairer to poorer students.
Entrance examinations test only genuine understanding and cannot be prepared for.

steps: The paragraph describes how coaching has changed entrance examinations and records a suggested remedy; the correct option includes both.
"Fairer to poorer students" contradicts the point about ability to pay; the hubs option is one detail.
solution.trap: Abolition by lottery goes far beyond "reducing the stakes of a single examination".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Over the past decade, several smaller public sector banks in India have been merged into larger ones. Supporters argue that bigger banks can spread their costs over more customers, invest more in technology and lend to large projects that smaller banks could not finance alone. Critics point out that mergers do not by themselves fix weak lending practices, and that combining the systems, staff and working cultures of different banks can disrupt service for years. The evidence so far is mixed: some merged banks have become stronger, while others are still struggling with integration. Much depends on how well each merger is managed after it is announced.
options: Mergers have made every public sector bank stronger.
Bigger banks can invest more in technology.
Public sector banks should be sold to private owners instead of being merged.
Mergers have been a complete failure and should be reversed.
Bank mergers promise benefits of scale but carry integration risks and do not by themselves fix weak lending, so results so far have been mixed and depend on how each merger is managed.

steps: The paragraph weighs arguments for and against mergers and reports mixed results; the correct option keeps that balance.
"Every bank stronger" and "complete failure" each take one side of mixed evidence.
solution.trap: The technology option is only one of the supporters' points.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Gross domestic product measures the value of the goods and services an economy produces, and it is often treated as a measure of national well-being. It was never designed for that purpose. GDP rises when a forest is cut down and sold as timber, but it records no loss for the forest itself. It counts spending on treating pollution-related illness as output, while ignoring the unpaid work of caring for children and the elderly. None of this makes GDP useless; it remains an essential gauge of economic activity. The error lies in mistaking a measure of activity for a measure of welfare.
options: GDP is a misleading statistic and should be abandoned.
GDP is a valuable gauge of economic activity, but because it ignores environmental losses and unpaid work and counts some harms as gains, it should not be mistaken for a measure of well-being.
GDP counts spending on pollution-related illness as economic output.
Countries should replace GDP with an index of happiness.
GDP is the best available measure of a nation's well-being.

steps: The paragraph defends GDP as a measure of activity while rejecting its use as a measure of welfare; the correct option carries both halves.
"Should be abandoned" ignores the concession "None of this makes GDP useless".
solution.trap: The happiness index is a common proposal elsewhere, but the paragraph never makes it.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

It seems obvious that making appliances and vehicles more energy-efficient will reduce the total energy a society uses. The historical record is less reassuring. When a technology becomes more efficient, the cost of using it falls, and people often respond by using it more: efficient air-conditioners are run for longer, and cars that use less fuel are driven farther. In some cases the extra use cancels much of the saving. This does not mean that efficiency is pointless. It means that efficiency alone cannot be relied on to cut energy use unless it is combined with measures, such as pricing, that discourage the added consumption.
options: Because efficiency lowers the cost of using energy, it can encourage extra use that offsets the savings, so it must be combined with measures such as pricing if consumption is to fall.
Energy-efficient appliances increase total energy use and should not be promoted.
Cars that use less fuel tend to be driven farther.
Efficiency improvements always reduce a society's total energy use.
Governments should ban air-conditioners in order to save energy.

steps: The paragraph argues that efficiency gains can be eaten up by extra use, so they must be paired with measures like pricing; the correct option states the mechanism and the conclusion.
"Should not be promoted" contradicts "This does not mean that efficiency is pointless".
solution.trap: The cars option is only one example of the rebound effect.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Economists increasingly argue that a country's prosperity depends less on its natural resources than on the quality of its institutions. Where contracts are enforced quickly and fairly, businesses are willing to trade with strangers, lend money and invest for the long term. Where disputes drag on for years, firms deal only with people they know, keep their operations small and demand payment in advance. Much potential trade simply never happens. In India, commercial cases can take several years to resolve, which quietly raises the cost of doing business. Speeding up the courts may therefore do as much for growth as many more visible reforms.
options: Natural resources play no part in a country's prosperity.
Prosperity depends heavily on institutions such as swift contract enforcement, and since slow courts raise business costs in India, speeding them up could do much for growth.
Commercial cases in India can take several years to resolve.
India should set up special courts staffed by retired judges.
Firms prefer to deal only with people they know, whatever the legal system.

steps: The paragraph moves from a general claim (institutions drive prosperity) to its application (speed up India's courts); the correct option has both.
"No part" overstates "depends less on", and the delays option is only the Indian example.
solution.trap: The last option drops the condition: firms deal only with people they know where disputes drag on.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Social media platforms show each user a feed chosen by algorithms that learn what holds his attention. The aim is commercial, not political: the longer people stay, the more advertisements they see. But content that provokes anger or fear tends to hold attention best, so it is shown more often. Over time, users may see a narrower and more extreme picture of the world than the one they would meet in a newspaper, not because anyone planned it but because the system rewards engagement. Some researchers argue that platforms should be required to explain how their feeds work and to let users choose simpler, chronological ones.
options: Social media companies deliberately design their feeds to spread political propaganda.
The longer users stay on social media, the more advertisements they see.
People should stop using social media and read only newspapers.
Algorithms show users a balanced picture of the world.
Because feed algorithms reward engagement and anger holds attention, users may be shown a distorted picture of the world without anyone intending it, prompting calls for transparency and user choice.

steps: The paragraph explains how an attention-driven system can distort users' view without design, and notes proposed remedies; the correct option has the mechanism, the unintended effect and the remedy.
The advertisements option is only the commercial motive.
solution.trap: "Deliberately … propaganda" contradicts "commercial, not political" and "not because anyone planned it".

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Official figures say that about a third of Indians live in urban areas, but this may understate the country's real urbanisation. Many large villages have tens of thousands of residents, dense housing and most people working outside agriculture, yet they are still governed as villages. Because they lack municipal status, they receive none of the funds and planning powers that towns enjoy, and their roads, drains and water supply fall far short of what their populations need.
