Recognising such places as urban, researchers argue, is not a matter of statistics alone; it would allow them to be planned and serviced as the towns they have effectively become.
options: Most Indians now live in cities, whatever the official figures say.
Large villages lack proper roads, drains and water supply.
Villages should be prevented from growing into towns.
Reclassifying villages as towns would change only the official statistics.
Many large villages are urban in all but name, and classifying them as towns would give them the funding and planning their growth needs, not merely change the statistics.

steps: The paragraph argues that many villages are really towns and that recognising them would bring planning and services; the correct option gives both the claim and its practical point.
"Only the statistics" contradicts "not a matter of statistics alone".
solution.trap: "May understate" does not mean "most Indians live in cities"; that option overstates the claim.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Crop insurance is meant to protect farmers from ruin when harvests fail, yet many farmers who have paid premiums complain that claims are settled late or not at all. Part of the problem lies in how losses are measured. Because it is costly to inspect every field, payouts are usually based on sample harvests across a whole area, so a farmer whose crop is destroyed may receive nothing if the area average looks normal. Delays in conducting these sample harvests and in releasing governments' shares of premiums slow payments further. Satellite data and smartphone-based crop assessments could make measurement faster and more precise, restoring farmers' faith in the scheme.
options: Insurance companies deliberately refuse to pay farmers' claims to increase their profits.
It is too costly to inspect every farmer's field.
Farmers should stop paying premiums for crop insurance.
Crop insurance often fails individual farmers because losses are measured by area-wide samples and payments are delayed, and technology could make assessment quicker and more accurate.
Crop insurance pays each farmer exactly for his own loss.

steps: The paragraph traces farmers' complaints to how losses are measured and to delays, then proposes technology; the correct option has the causes and the remedy.
"Exactly for his own loss" contradicts the area-average method.
solution.trap: The first option supplies a motive (profit) the paragraph never mentions; it blames measurement methods and delays.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Historians often rely on sources that were never meant to be neutral. Royal inscriptions praise the rulers who commissioned them, and court chronicles celebrate victories while passing over defeats. Reading such material as a plain record would produce a flattering and distorted picture of the past. Yet historians do not throw these sources away, because for many periods little else survives. They compare them with other evidence, such as coins, travellers' accounts and archaeological finds, and they read them for what they reveal unintentionally: the titles a king claimed, for instance, show what his subjects were expected to admire. Biased sources, handled critically, can still be rich evidence.
options: Historians should rely only on archaeological finds, because written sources are biased.
Royal inscriptions praise the rulers who commissioned them.
Although many historical sources are biased, historians can still draw valuable evidence from them by cross-checking them and reading them critically for what they reveal unintentionally.
Court chronicles give an accurate record of both victories and defeats.
Most of what we know about ancient kings is false.

steps: The paragraph admits the bias of the sources but argues they remain useful when handled critically; the correct option keeps the concession and the conclusion.
The archaeology option contradicts "historians do not throw these sources away".
solution.trap: "Most of what we know is false" turns a warning about reading sources carelessly into a sweeping verdict.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Regulators of new technologies face a timing problem. Early on, when a technology is still flexible and rules could shape it easily, too little is known about its effects to regulate it wisely. By the time the harms become clear, the technology is embedded in industries and daily life, and changing it is costly and contested. Waiting for certainty therefore has its own risks. Some scholars suggest that regulators adopt provisional rules that are reviewed as evidence builds up, together with requirements that companies share data on how their products are used, so that policy can adjust before it is too late.
options: Regulators should ban new technologies until their effects are fully understood.

Since new technologies are easiest to regulate before their effects are known and hardest afterwards, regulators could adopt provisional, reviewable rules and require companies to share data so that policy adjusts in time.
Once a technology is part of daily life, changing it is costly.
Regulators should wait until they are certain before making any rules.
Technology companies always hide the harms their products cause.

steps: The paragraph sets out the dilemma of timing and a proposed way through it; the correct option has both.
"Wait until certain" is the approach the paragraph says "has its own risks", and a ban is not proposed.
solution.trap: The daily-life option states only one side of the dilemma.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Dense cities are often blamed for congestion, pollution and crowding, and many planners respond by limiting building heights and spreading development outwards. The effects can be the opposite of those intended. Low-rise sprawl pushes homes far from jobs, lengthening commutes and increasing car use. It makes public transport harder to run profitably, since fewer people live near each station, and it swallows farmland at the city's edge. Roads, pipes and power lines must also be stretched over far greater distances. Density itself is not the problem; poorly planned density, without adequate transport, open space and services, is. Well-managed compact cities can be greener and more efficient than sprawling ones.
options: Cities should remove all limits on the height of buildings.
Low-rise sprawl swallows farmland at the edge of cities.
Dense cities are the main cause of pollution and crowding.
Restricting density to avoid congestion can backfire by encouraging sprawl; the real problem is poorly planned density, and well-managed compact cities can be greener and more efficient.
Most people prefer to live in suburbs rather than in city centres.

steps: The paragraph argues that limiting density backfires and that the real issue is planning; the correct option captures both claims.
The third option repeats the view the paragraph rejects; the farmland option is one effect of sprawl.
solution.trap: Removing all height limits is more than the paragraph says; it calls for well-managed density with transport and services.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Randomised trials, in which one group receives a programme and a similar group does not, have become a popular way to test whether development schemes work. Their appeal is clarity: because the groups differ only in whether they received the programme, any difference in outcomes can be credited to it. Critics note, however, that a result from one district or one year may not hold elsewhere, where conditions differ, and that trials can answer only narrow questions that lend themselves to testing. Randomised trials are thus a powerful tool, but their findings need to be combined with other evidence and local knowledge before they guide national policy.
options: Randomised trials are the only reliable way to evaluate development schemes.
Randomised trials are unreliable and should not be used.
In a randomised trial, one group receives a programme and another does not.

Randomised trials give clear evidence on whether a programme works, but because results may not transfer and the questions they answer are narrow, they should be combined with other evidence before guiding policy.
National policy should be decided by local officials alone.

steps: The paragraph praises the clarity of trials, states their limits and concludes they should be combined with other evidence; the correct option carries all three.
"Only reliable way" and "should not be used" each take one half of a balanced view.
solution.trap: The definition option describes a trial but says nothing about the argument.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

Water in Indian cities is usually priced far below the cost of supplying it. The intention is to protect the poor, but the effect is often the reverse. Utilities that cannot recover their costs lack money to extend pipelines, so the poorest neighbourhoods remain unconnected and buy water from private tankers at many times the official rate. Meanwhile, better-off households with piped connections enjoy cheap water and have little reason to save it. Some reformers propose charging higher rates for heavy use while keeping a basic amount free or very cheap, so that utilities can expand their networks without burdening poor families.
options: Water should be supplied free of cost to every city household.
Poor households buy water from tankers at many times the official rate.
Underpricing city water, meant to help the poor, starves utilities of funds, leaving the poor unconnected and paying more; higher rates for heavy use with a cheap basic allowance could fix this.
Cheap water has helped poor families more than any other group.
Private companies should take over water supply in all cities.

steps: The paragraph shows how a pro-poor price backfires and proposes a tiered tariff; the correct option has the irony and the remedy.
The tanker option is one consequence; "helped poor families more than any other group" reverses the argument.
solution.trap: Free water for all is the opposite of the reform the paragraph describes.

items.prompt:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best summarises it.

For decades, companies organised their supply chains for efficiency, buying each component from whichever supplier in the world could make it most cheaply and keeping stocks to a minimum. The approach cut costs, but it left little margin for shocks. When a pandemic closed factories or a single ship blocked a canal, production lines thousands of kilometres away halted for want of a few parts. Many firms are now building in resilience by keeping larger stocks and sourcing key components from more than one country. This costs more in normal times, but companies increasingly see it as insurance worth paying for.
options: Companies are abandoning global trade and making everything at home.
A single ship blocking a canal halted production in distant factories.
Keeping larger stocks lowers companies' costs in normal times.
Governments should subsidise companies that keep large stocks.
Supply chains built purely for low cost proved fragile in shocks, so firms are now accepting higher everyday costs for resilience through larger stocks and more than one supplier.

steps: The paragraph contrasts efficiency-first supply chains with the new focus on resilience, and the trade-off involved; the correct option captures the shift and its cost.
"Making everything at home" distorts "sourcing … from more than one country"; the ship option is one example.
solution.trap: The stocks option reverses "This costs more in normal times".
